<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|way|6855|way}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''6.''' Pursuit; calling; line of business. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|Men of his ''way'' should be most liberal.
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., i. 3. 61.}}}}
{{smaller block|Thinking that this would prove a busy day in the justicing ''way'', I am come, Sir Jacob, to lend you a hand.
{{right|''Foote'', Mayor of Garratt, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|Is not Gus Hoskins, my brother-in-law, partner with his excellent father in the leather ''way?''
{{right|''Thackeray'', Great Hoggarty Diamond, xiii.}}}}

'''7.''' Respect; point or particular: with ''in'' expressed or understood.
{{smaller block|You wrong me every ''way''. {{right|''Shak.'', J. C., iv. 3. 55.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The office of a man
That’s truly valiant is considerable,
Three ''ways:'' the first is in respect of matter.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', New Inn, iv. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|Thus farr, and many other ''waies'' were his Counsels and preparations before hand with us, either to a civil Warr, if it should happ’n, or to subdue us without a Warr.
{{right|''Milton'', Eikonoklastes, x.}}}}

'''8.''' Condition; state: as, he has recovered a little, but is still in a very bad ''way''. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|When ever you see a thorough Libertine, you may almost swear he is in a rising ''way'', and that the Poet intends to make him a great Man.
{{right|''Jeremy Collier'', Short View (ed. 1698), p. 211.}}}}
{{smaller block|You must tell him to keep up his spirits; everybody almost is in the same ''way''.
{{right|''Sheridan'', School for Scandal, i. 1.}}}}

'''9.''' Course of action or procedure; means by which anything is to be reached, attained, or accomplished; scheme; device; plan; course.
{{smaller block|Of Taxations, properly so called, there were never fewer in any King’s Reign; but of ''Ways'' to draw Money from the Subject, never more. {{right|''Baker'', Chronicles, p. 66.}}}}
<poem>By noble ''ways'' we conquest will prepare;
First offer peace, and, that refused, make war.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Dryden'', Indian Emperor, i. 1.}}}}

'''10.''' Method or manner of proceeding; mode; style; fashion; wise: as, the right or the wrong ''way'' of doing something.
{{smaller block|God hath so many times and ''ways'' spoken to men.
{{right|''Hooker.''}}}}
{{smaller block|I will one ''way'' or other make you amends.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., iii. 1. 89.}}}}
{{smaller block|One would imagine the Ethiopians either had two alphabets, or that they had two ''ways'' of writing most things.
{{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, I. 227.}}}}
{{smaller block|This answerer had, in a ''way'' not to be pardoned, drawn his pen against a certain great man then alive.
{{right|''Swift'', Tale of a Tub, Apol.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Thou say’st an undisputed thing
In such a solemn ''way''.</poem>
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', To an Insect.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>’Tis not so much the gallant who woos,
As the gallant’s ''way'' of wooing!</poem>
{{right|''W. S. Gilbert'', Way of Wooing.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Way'' in this sense is equivalent to ''wise'', and in certain colloquial phrases is confused with it, appearing in the apparent plural ''ways'', which really represents ''wise'': as, no ''ways'', length''ways'', end''ways'', etc.}}
{{smaller block|To him [God] we can not exhibit ouermuch praise, nor belye him any ''wayes'', vnlesse it be in abasing his excellencie by scarsitie of praise.
{{right|''Puttenham'', Arte of Eng. Poesie, p. 22.}}}}
{{smaller block|He could no ''way'' stir.
{{right|''Bacon'', Physical Fables, ii.}}}}
{{smaller block|Hee at that time could be no ''way'' esteem’d the Father of his Countrey, but the destroyer.
{{right|''Milton'', Eikonoklastes, xxi.}}}}
{{smaller block|Simon Glendinning . . . bit the dust, no ''way'' disparaging in his death that ancient race from which he claimed his descent.
{{right|''Scott'', Monastery, ii.}}}}

'''11.''' Regular or usual method or manner, as in acting or speaking; habitual or peculiar mode or manner of doing or saying things: as, that is only his ''way''; an odd ''way'' he has; women’s ''ways''.
{{smaller block|<poem>We call it only pretty Fanny’s ''way''.</poem>
{{right|''Parnell'', Elegy to an Old Beauty.}}}}
{{smaller block|It is my ''way'' to write down all the good things I have heard in the last conversation, to furnish my paper.
{{right|''Steele'', Tatler, No. 45.}}}}
{{smaller block|Before I departed, the good priest ask’d me my name, that they might pray in the church for my good journey, which is only a ''way'' they have of desiring charity.
{{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, I. 138.}}}}
{{smaller block|He was imperious sometimes still; but I did not mind that; I saw it was his ''way''.
{{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Jane Eyre, xv.}}}}
{{smaller block|All her little womanly ''ways'', budding out of her like blossoms on a young fruit-tree.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Seven Gables, ix.}}}}
'''12.''' Resolved plan or mode of action or conduct; a course insisted upon as one’s own.
{{smaller block|<poem>If I had my ''way''
He had mewed in flames at home. ''B. Jonson.''</poem>
<poem>Man has his will—but woman has her ''way''!</poem>
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', A Prologue.}}}}
{{smaller block|If Lord Durham had had his ''way'', the Ballot would at that time [1833] have been included in the programme of the Government.
{{right|''J. McCarthy'', Hist. Own Times, I. 54.}}}}
'''13.''' Circuit or range of action or observation.
{{smaller block|The general officers and the public ministers that fell in my ''way'' were generally subject to the gout.
{{right|''Sir W. Temple.''}}}}

'''14.''' Progress; advancement.
{{smaller block|Socialism in any systematic or definite form, as a scheme for superseding the institution of Capital, had not in my opinion made any serious ''way''.
{{right|''Nineteenth Century'', XXVI. 730.}}}}

'''15.''' ''Naut.'', progress or motion through the water; headway: as, a vessel is under ''way'' when she begins to move, she gathers ''way'' when her rate of sailing increases, and loses ''way'' when it diminishes.
{{smaller block|Towards night it grew very calm and a great fog, so as our ships made no ''way''.
{{right|''Winthrop'', Hist. New England, I. 8.}}}}
{{smaller block|Soundings are usually taken from the vessel, and while there is some ''way'' on.
{{right|''Sir C. W. Thomson'', Depths of the Sea, p. 206.}}}}
{{smaller block|A ship, so long as she can keep ''way'' on her, and can steer, need not fear an enemy’s ram.
{{right|''Sci. Amer.'', N. S., LXIII. 304.}}}}

'''16.''' ''pl.'' In ''mach.'', etc., the line or course along which anything worked on is caused to move. See cut under ''shaper''. {{smaller|(''a'') The timbers on which a ship is launched: as, a new ship on the ''ways''. See cut under ''launching-way''. (''b'') Skids on which weights, barrels, etc., are moved up or down, as on an inclined plane.—'''A furlong way†.''' See ''furlong''.—'''A lion in the way.''' See ''lion''.—'''Appian Way.''' See ''Appian''.—'''A way of necessity,''' a way which the law allows for passage to and from land not otherwise accessible. It arises only over one of two parcels of land of both of which the grantor was the owner when he conveyed the other; and it arises in favor of the parcel conveyed when this is wholly surrounded by what had been the grantor’s other land, or partly by this and partly by that of a stranger.—'''By all ways†,''' in all respects; in every way.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>My lady gaf me al hooly
The noble gift of her mercy,
Saving her worship, ''by alle weyes''.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Death of Blanche, l. 1271.}}}} By the way. See ''by''<sup>1</sup>.—'''By way of''', for the purpose of; to serve as. See also ''by''<sup>1</sup>.

{{smaller block|The Kyng of that Contree, ones every zeer, zevethe leve to pore men to gon in to the Lake, to gadre hem precyous Stones and Perles, ''be weye of'' Alemesse, for the love of God, that made Adam. {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 199.}}}}

{{smaller block|That this gift of perpetual youth should pass from men to serpents seems added ''by way of'' ornament. {{right|''Bacon'', Physical Fables, ii., Expl.}}}}

'''By way of being, doing''', etc., in the condition of being, doing, etc.; so as to be, do, etc. [Eng.]—'''Come your ways.''' See ''come''.—'''Committee of Ways and Means.''' (''a'') In the British Parliament, a committee of the whole house which considers the ways and means of raising the supplies. (''b'') One of the most important of the standing committees of the United States House of Representatives: to it are referred bills relating to the raising of the revenue.—'''Common way.''' See ''common''.—'''Covered way.''' See ''cover''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Direct way around, dry way, Dunstable way.''' See the adjectives.—'''High way.''' See ''highway''.—'''In a small way.''' See ''small''.—'''In the family way.''' See ''family''.—'''In the way.''' (''a'') Along the road; on the way; as one proceeds.

<poem>And as we wenten thus ''in the weye'' wordyng togyderes,
Thanne seye we a Samaritan sittende on a mule,
Rydynge ful rapely the riȝt weye we ȝeden.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), xvii. 47.}}}}

{{smaller block|The next morning, going to Cumæ through a very pleasant path, by the Mare Mortuum and the Elysian Fields, we saw ''in our way'' a great many ruins of sepulchres and other ancient edifices. {{right|''Addison'', Remarks on Italy (ed. Bohn), I. 452.}}}}

(''b'') On hand; present.

{{smaller block|When your master or lady calls a servant by name, if that servant be not ''in the way'', none of you are to answer. {{right|''Swift'', Advice to Servants (General Directions).}}}}
{{smaller block|(''c'') In such a position or of such a nature as to obstruct, impede, or hinder: as, a meddler is always ''in the way;'' there are difficulties ''in the way.''}}

{{smaller block|I never seemed ''in his way;'' he did not take fits of chilling hauteur; when he met me unexpectedly, the encounter seemed welcome — he had always a word and sometimes a smile for me. {{right|''Charlotte Brontë,'' Jane Eyre, xv.}}}}

'''In the way of.''' {{smaller|(''a'') So as to meet or fall in with; in a favorable position for doing or getting: as, I can put you ''in the way of'' a profitable investment. (''b'') In the matter or business of; as regards; in respect of.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>What my tongue can do
''I’ the way of'' flattery.</poem>{{right|''Shak.,'' Cor., iii. 2. 137.}}}}

'''Mean way†.''' {{smaller|See ''mean''<sup>3</sup>.}}—'''Milky Way.''' {{smaller|See ''Galaxy,'' 1.}}—'''Once in a way.''' {{smaller|See ''once''<sup>1</sup>.}}—'''On the way,''' {{smaller|in going or traveling along; hence, in progress or advance toward completion or accomplishment.}}
{{smaller block|My lord, I over-rode him ''on the way.''{{right|''Shak.,'' 2 Hen. IV., i. 1. 30.}}}}

'''Out of the way.''' {{smaller|(''a'') Out of the road or path; so as not to obstruct or hinder.}}
{{smaller block|Take up the stumblingblock ''out of the way'' of my people.{{right|Isa. lvii. 14.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') At a distance from; clear of: as, to keep ''out of the way'' of a carriage.}}
{{smaller block|The embroylments and factions that were then amongst the Arabs . . . made us desirous to keep as far as possible ''out of'' their ''way.'' {{right|''Maundrell,'' Aleppo to Jerusalem, p. 56.}}}}
{{smaller|(''c'') Not in the proper course; in such a position or condition as to miss one’s object; away from the mark; aside; astray; hence, improper; wrong.}}
{{smaller block|We are quite ''out of the way'' when we think that things contain within themselves the qualities that appear to us in them. {{right|''Locke.''}}}}

{{smaller block|He that knows but a little of them [matters of speculation or practice], and is very confident of his own strength, is more ''out of the way'' of true knowledge than if he knew nothing at all. {{right|''Bp. Atterbury'', Sermons, I. v.}}}}
(''d'') Not in its proper place, or where it can be found or met with; hence, mislaid, hidden, or lost.
{{smaller block|Is ’t lost? is ’t gone? speak, is it ''out o’ the way?'' {{right|''Shak.'', Othello, iii. 4. 80.}}}}
(''e'') Out of the beaten track; not in the usual, ordinary, or regular course; hence, extraordinary; remarkable: as, her accomplishments are nothing ''out of the way:'' often used attributively. Compare ''to put one’s self out of the way'', below.
{{smaller block|This seemed to us then to be a place ''out of the way'', where we might lye snug for a while. {{right|''Dampier'', Voyages, I. 389.}}}}
{{smaller block|It is probable they formerly had some staple commodity here, and that they bestowed great expences on their public games, in order to make people resort to a place which was so much ''out of the way''. {{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, II. ii. 71.}}}} '''Permanent way''', in ''rail.'', a finished road-bed and track including switches, crossings, bridges, viaducts, etc., as distinguished from a ''temporary way'', such as is used in construction, in removing the soil of cuttings, etc.—'''Private way''', a right which one or more persons, as distinguished from the public generally, have of passing to and fro across land of another. It may exist by grant, by long usage, or by proceedings, sanctioned by law in some states, to acquire a necessary access and egress on making compensation.—'''Right of way.''' (''a'') A right to pass and repass over real property of another. (''b'') The right to pass over a path or way, to the temporary exclusion of others: as, an express-train has the ''right of way'' as against a freight-train. (''c'') The strip of land of which a railway-company acquires either the ownership or the use for the laying of its tracks.—'''Second covered way''', in ''fort.'', the way beyond the second ditch.—'''The Way''', in the New Testament, the Christian religion or church; Christianity. The phrase is rendered in the authorized version (except once) “this way” or “that way”; in the revised version (except Acts xxii. 4, where it has the demonstrative “this”), “the Way.” Acts ix. 2; xix. 9, 23; xxii. 4; xxiv. 14, 22.—'''To break a way.''' See ''break.''—'''To clear the way.''' See ''clear.''—'''To devour the way.''' See ''devour''<sup>1</sup>.—'''To gather way.''' See ''gather.''—'''To give way''', to grant passage; allow to pass; hence, to yield: generally with ''to''.
{{smaller block|Open your gates and ''give'' the victors ''way.''
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, ii. 1. 324.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>They happen’d to meet on a long narrow bridge,
And neither of them would ''give way.''</poem>
{{right|''Robin Hood and Little John'' (Child’s Ballads, V. 217).}}}}
{{smaller block|We ''give'' too much ''way to'' our passions.
{{right|''Burton'', Anat. of Mel., p. 329.}}}}
{{smaller block|Suetonius, though else a worthie man, overproud of his Victorie, ''gave'' too much ''way to'' his anger against the Britans. {{right|''Milton'', Hist. Eng., ii.}}}}
{{smaller block|The senate, forced to yield to the tribunes of the people, thought it their wisest course also to ''give way to'' the time.
{{right|''Swift.''}}}}

'''To go one’s way''' or '''ways.''' See ''go.''—'''To go the way of all the earth,''' to die. 1 Ki. ii. 2.—'''To go the way of nature.''' See ''nature.''—'''To have one’s way.''' See def. 12.—'''To keep way†,''' to keep pace.
{{smaller block|When there be not stonds [stops] and restiveness in a man’s nature, . . . the wheels of his mind ''keep way'' with the wheels of his fortune. {{right|''Bacon'', Fortune (ed. 1887).}}}}
'''To labor on the way.''' See ''labor''<sup>1</sup>.—'''To lead the way,''' to be the first or most forward in a march, progress, or the like; act the part of a leader, guide, etc.
{{smaller block|<poem>He tried each art, reproved each dull delay,
Allured to brighter worlds, and ''led the way.''</poem>
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Des. Vil., l. 170.}}}}
'''To lie in the''' or '''one’s way.''' See ''lie''<sup>1</sup>.—'''To look both ways for Sunday,''' to squint. [Colloq.]—'''To look nine ways.''' See ''nine.''—'''To lose way.''' See ''lose''<sup>1</sup>.—'''To make one’s way.''' See ''make''<sup>1</sup>.—'''To make the best of one’s way.''' See ''best.''—'''To make way.''' (''a'') To give room for passing; give place; stand aside to permit another to pass.
{{smaller block|Ther was no romayn so hardy ne so myghty but he ''made'' hym ''wey.'' {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), iii. 655.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Make way'' there for the princess.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., v. 4. 91.}}}}
{{smaller block|The petty squadrons which had till now harassed the coast of Britain ''made way'' for hosts larger than had fallen on any country in the west.
{{right|''J. R. Green'', Conq. of Eng., p. 84.}}}}
(''b'') To open a path through obstacles; overcome resistance, hindrance, or difficulties.
{{smaller block|<poem>With this little arm and this good sword,
I have ''made'' my ''way'' through more impediments
Than twenty times your stop.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, v. 2. 263.}}}}
(''c'') To advance; move forward.
{{smaller block|We, seeing them prepare to assault vs, left our Oares and ''made way'' with our sayle to incounter them.
{{right|Quoted in ''Capt. John Smith’s'' Works, I. 181.}}}}

'''To pave the way.''' See ''pave.''—'''To put one’s self out of the way,''' to give one’s self trouble.
{{smaller block|Don’t ''put yourself out of the way'', on our accounts.
{{right|''Dickens'', Oliver Twist, xxxi.}}}}
'''To take one’s way.''' (''a'') To set out; go.
{{smaller block|<poem>They, hand in hand, with wandering steps and slow,
Through Eden ''took'' their solitary ''way''.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., xii. 649.}}}}
(''b'') To follow one’s own plan, opinion, inclination, or fancy.
{{smaller block|<poem>Doctor, your service for this time is ended;
''Take your'' own ''way''.    ''Shak.'', Cymbeline, i. 5. 31.</poem>}}
'''Under way,''' in progress; in motion: said of a vessel that has weighed her anchor or has left her moorings and is making progress through the water; hence, generally, making progress; having started: often erroneously writ-<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
